entry.title: AWS SQS FIFO vs Standard Queues for Healthtech Payment Retry Design
entry.summary: Short answer: Use Standard for independently idempotent nightly snapshot jobs; use FIFO only when per-entity ordering or queue deduplication is a real invariant. For a nightly healthtech payment reconciliation, choose queue semantics from the failure boundary you need to preserve, not from the retry count. Standard delivery fits work that is independently safe to repeat and does not require ordering. FIFO fits work that must remain ordered within a message group and benefits from queue-supported deduplication. The invariant is narrower than exactly once: a clinic and settlement window produce one durable reconciliation result, a retry carries the same key, and a duplicate message cannot create a second ledger adjustment. Introduction
Developers transitioning from Java or Rust to Go often encounter puzzling behaviors rooted in Go's unique handling of struct copying and pointer semantics. entry.title: MySQL to PostgreSQL Schema Conversion: What Each Column Type Should Become, and What Silently Changes
entry.summary: Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples. TL;DR: Most MySQL types have an obvious PostgreSQL twin, but eight need a decision: TINYINT(1), UNSIGNED integers, DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP, ENUM, SET, ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, AUTO_INCREMENT and the collation behind every unique text column. Converting a MySQL schema to PostgreSQL is mostly mechanical, and the parts that are not mechanical are the ones that break production. The Workflow That Paged Me 47 Times: Deduplicating n8n Failure Alerts
This is part of my build-in-public series on running LLM workflows in n8n in production. Everything here is from real templates I sell and support — the mistakes are mine, the fixes are tested. One night a provider went down, and my phone paged me forty-seven times. Not forty-seven failures. One failure, retried and re-alerted until the provider came back up in the morning. Each retry produced a new execution, each execution hit the same dead provider, and each one fired its own alert. By page twelve I had stopped reading them. By page thirty I had muted the channel.
